title: Cypriot Greek: the most widely spoken dialect
status: Vigorous, in a continuum with Standard Greek
lead: If you land in Larnaca speaking textbook Greek, you will be understood perfectly and answered in something you only half follow: **«Ίντα που θέλεις;»**, **«εν ξέρω»**, **«τζαι»** for **και**. Cypriot is the one Greek dialect that is a living everyday language for a whole country, around 700,000 people. It is not a descendant of the ancient Arcadocypriot dialect of the island: like almost every modern dialect it grew out of the Koine. But centuries of separation, first under Arab raids and then under Frankish, Venetian, Ottoman and British rule, let it keep old features the mainland lost and build new ones of its own.
facts: Cyprus, with large communities in London, Australia and elsewhere; regional varieties differ (Paphos, Larnaca, Famagusta, the mountains).
About 700,000 Greek Cypriots. In 1960, 38% of Turkish Cypriots could also speak Greek.
South-eastern, with the Dodecanese, Chios and parts of the Cyclades.
From the 14th century: the Assizes, the chronicles of Leontios Machairas (15th c.) and Georgios Boustronios (16th c.), and a 16th-century collection of love poems.
Standard Greek is the official language of school, law and news; Cypriot is the language of home, street, radio talk shows, comedy and rap.

timeline.text: Cyprus spoke **Arcadocypriot**, written in a syllabary. It died out in the Hellenistic period, replaced by the Koine, the true ancestor of Cypriot.

Arab raids from 647 lead to a **condominium**: the island pays taxes to both Byzantium and the Caliphate. Three centuries of relative isolation, when Cypriot speech probably began to diverge from the Greek of the centre.

The French **Lusignan** kingdom. Greek remains the language of the people, French of the court. The **Assizes**, the law code, are translated into Cypriot Greek, and Machairas writes his chronicle in it, full of French and Italian words.
Ottoman rule. Turkish loans enter everyday speech, and many Turkish Cypriots grow up bilingual.
British administration and then colony. English becomes the language of government; English loans follow.

Independence, then the 1974 division. Standard Greek is used for education and official life, and a common **urban Cypriot koine**, based on the speech of Nicosia and the Mesaoria plain, levels the village differences.

sections.after: Glide hardening is the feature that most puzzles mainland ears. Where standard Greek has a short **ι** before another vowel (καρδ**ιά**), Cypriot turns it into a consonant: [kaɾˈca], spelled **καρκιά**.

sections.h: Syntax: the pronoun after the verb
sections.text: Cypriot places the weak pronoun **after** the verb in ordinary statements, as medieval Greek did. It also builds questions with **ίντα** 'what' as a cleft: literally 'what is it that…'.

examples.en: What did you see? (lit. what is it that you saw?)
Send it to me: indirect object first.
What you say is right: **τα** as a relative 'what'.

sections.after: Cypriot also has local loans from Old French, Italian and English that the mainland never took. London Cypriots have added English words that the island itself does not use.

sections.text: Greek Cypriots grow up with two varieties. **Standard Modern Greek** is the language of the state, the school and the news; **Cypriot** is learned at home and stands for intimacy, humour and Cypriot identity. Linguists such as Spiros Moschonas (1996) describe this as **diglossia**. In practice speakers move along a continuum: at one end the Standard as spoken in Cyprus, at the other the village dialect, and in the middle the urban Cypriot koine, which keeps only the most basic Cypriot features. For a learner from Greece, the koine is the variety you will meet.

sample.intro: The national poem of Cyprus, written in the dialect around 1884–1895. It tells of the execution of Archbishop Kyprianos by the Ottoman authorities in 1821. Stanza 18 and the close of stanza 19.
lines: Η Ρωμιοσύνη εν φυλή συνότζαιρη του κόσμου,
κανένας δεν εβρέθηκεν για να την ι-ξηλείψη,
κανένας, γιατί σιέπει την που τα 'ψη ο Θεός μου.
Η Ρωμιοσύνη εν να χαθή, όντες ο κόσμος λείψει!
Σφάξε μας ούλους τζι ας γενεί το γαίμαν μας αυλάτζιν,
αμμά ξέρε πως ύλαντρον όντες κοπεί καβάτζιν
en: Greekness is a race as old as the world,
no one has ever been found to wipe it out,
no one, because my God shields it from on high.
Greekness will vanish only when the world ends!
Slaughter us all and let our blood become a stream,
but know that when a tree is cut down at the stump,
three hundred new shoots burst out around it.
sample.source: Vasilis Michaelides (1849–1917), public domain; text and translation after the Wikipedia article «Cypriot Greek».

culture.text: At weddings and festivals, Cypriot **ποιητάρηδες** improvise **τσιαττιστά**: rhyming couplets thrown back and forth as challenges, compliments and insults, each singer answering the last line of the other. UNESCO added tsiattista to its list of Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2011. The poet Dimitris Lipertis wrote much-loved lyric poems in the dialect, and today Cypriot is heard in comedy shows, local TV series and rap.

questions.q: Which ancient dialect is modern Cypriot descended from?
questions.why: Arcadocypriot died out in Hellenistic times; Cypriot, like nearly all modern dialects, grew from the Koine.

questions.q: How do you say «Δεν ξέρω» in Cypriot?

questions.why: **έννα** is the Cypriot future particle, standard **θα**.

questions.q: What does «καρκιά» correspond to in the standard?
questions.why: Glide hardening turns the [j] of καρδιά into [c].

questions.q: «Γράφει το» puts the pronoun after the verb. In the standard you would say…
questions.why: The standard puts weak pronouns before a finite verb.

gloss.εν: εν — δεν ('not') or είναι ('is'); εν να = θα
gloss.Ρωμιοσύνη: Ρωμιοσύνη — the Greek (Romaic) people and identity
gloss.'ψη: ύψη — 'heights', που τα 'ψη = from on high
